prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that shotgun pleadings that fail to give defendants adequate notice of the claims against them should be dismissed.

Cite at least six decisions of the Eleventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Complaint Is a Shotgun Pleading That Fails to Give Defendant Fair Notice and Should Be Dismissed.**

Rule 8(a)(2) requires "a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief." Rule 10(b) requires a party to state its claims in separate, numbered paragraphs. Together, these rules require a complaint to give each defendant "adequate notice of the claims against them and the grounds upon which each claim rests." *Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Office*, 792 F.3d 1313, 1323 (11th Cir. 2015). A complaint that does not do so is a "shotgun pleading." The Eleventh Circuit has criticized this form of pleading for decades. *See Davis v. Coca-Cola Bottling Co. Consol.*, 516 F.3d 955, 979 (11th Cir. 2008); *Cramer v. Florida*, 117 F.3d 1258, 1263 (11th Cir. 1997).

*Weiland* identifies four rough categories of shotgun pleadings. 792 F.3d at 1321–23. The first is a complaint in which each count adopts the allegations of all preceding counts. The second is a complaint "replete with conclusory, vague, and immaterial facts not obviously connected to any particular cause of action." The third is a complaint that does not separate each cause of action into its own count. The fourth is a complaint that asserts multiple claims against multiple defendants without saying which defendant is responsible for which acts. *Id.* The common thread is that each category fails "to one degree or another" to give defendants notice. *Id.* at 1323.

The Complaint falls into several of these categories. [Insert record cites: e.g., Count II incorporates "all preceding paragraphs," including every earlier count; Counts __ and __ combine distinct theories of liability; and the Complaint attributes conduct to "Defendants" collectively.] The Eleventh Circuit has long held that incorporating every prior count into each later one is a hallmark of shotgun pleading. *Anderson v. Dist. Bd. of Trs. of Cent. Fla. Cmty. Coll.*, 77 F.3d 364, 366–67 (11th Cir. 1996). Under this practice, each successive count carries all of the earlier counts' allegations and legal theories, so "it is virtually impossible to know which allegations of fact are intended to support which claim(s) for relief." *Id.* at 366. *See also Strategic Income Fund, L.L.C. v. Spear, Leeds & Kellogg Corp.*, 305 F.3d 1293, 1295 & n.9 (11th Cir. 2002) (criticizing complaints that incorporate all preceding paragraphs and counts). Lumping several claims into one count, or several defendants into one allegation, creates the same problem. *Weiland*, 792 F.3d at 1322–23; *Magluta v. Samples*, 256 F.3d 1282, 1284 (11th Cir. 2001) (criticizing a lengthy complaint that left defendants unable to discern what was alleged against whom). Defendant cannot tell which facts support which claim, or which claims are directed at it. It therefore cannot frame a meaningful response, assert defenses, or assess the scope of discovery.

The harm is not limited to Defendant. Shotgun pleadings "exact an intolerable toll on the trial court's docket," and they "waste scarce judicial resources, inexorably broaden the scope of discovery, wreak havoc on appellate court dockets, and undermine the public's respect for the courts." *Jackson v. Bank of Am., N.A.*, 898 F.3d 1348, 1356–57 (11th Cir. 2018) (citations omitted); *see also Cramer*, 117 F.3d at 1263. For that reason, a district court has the inherent authority, and a duty, to police its docket. A court that sees a shotgun pleading should require repleading, with or without a motion. *Vibe Micro, Inc. v. Shabanets*, 878 F.3d 1291, 1294–95 (11th Cir. 2018); *Jackson*, 898 F.3d at 1357–58. Rule 8 and Rule 10(b) apply to every litigant, and a plaintiff's failure to comply with them cannot be excused. *See Paylor v. Hartford Fire Ins. Co.*, 748 F.3d 1117, 1125–26 (11th Cir. 2014).

Defendant recognizes that the ordinary course is to give a plaintiff one chance to replead. *Vibe Micro*, 878 F.3d at 1295. The Court should dismiss the Complaint on that basis. If [Plaintiff] has already been told of these deficiencies or has already amended once, dismissal with prejudice is warranted. *See Jackson*, 898 F.3d at 1358–59; *Davis*, 516 F.3d at 979. At a minimum, any repleading order should direct Plaintiff to:

- separate each cause of action into its own count;
- identify which defendant each count is asserted against;
- limit each count to the facts that support it; and
- stop incorporating prior counts wholesale.

*Weiland*, 792 F.3d at 1321–23.
